screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.subtitle: How your game decides, repeats, and responds

narration.text: Control flow is how your program decides what to do next and how many times to repeat an action. In games, control flow answers questions like: is the player alive, which menu option was chosen, or should we spawn another enemy? This chapter teaches the conditional statements you use to branch — if, else if, else, and switch — and the looping structures that repeat behavior — for, while, and do-while. You will also learn how break and continue change loop execution so you can stop early or skip an iteration. Concrete examples in this chapter include checking player health to show a status message, using a switch for menu choices like New Game or Quit, iterating a list of enemies with a for loop, and implementing a simple guess-the-number console game that uses a loop and conditional hints. By the end, you'll understand common mistakes like accidental assignment instead of comparison and infinite loops, and you'll be able to apply these tools to basic game logic in your Unreal projects. Think about a small scene in your head and imagine how these decisions and repetitions control what happens next.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Control flow structures let your game make decisions and repeat actions reliably, which is essential for interactivity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn four practical skills that you will use immediately in simple game code. First, you will implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else to direct program execution based on runtime values like player health or inventory. You will practice writing conditions that read clearly and avoid common mistakes such as using assignment instead of comparison. Second, you will use switch statements to handle distinct menu choices or action IDs efficiently. You will see how the break keyword prevents fall-through and why a default case is recommended. Third, you will construct for, while, and do-while loops to repeat tasks such as spawning enemies, iterating game entities, or running a simple main loop. Each loop type has clear use cases and pitfalls, like off-by-one errors and infinite loops. Fourth, you will apply break and continue to change loop behavior when you need to exit early or skip an iteration, for example skipping disabled enemies or stopping when a target is found. Each objective includes a practical coding example to connect the idea to game scenarios.

keyIdea.title: Skills to gain
keyIdea.text: Write conditionals and loops that control gameplay, handle menu choices, and manage repeated updates safely.

narration.text: These follow-up objectives focus on safe practice and applying control flow to game scenarios. You will learn to avoid the common pitfall of using the assignment operator instead of the equality operator when comparing values, which can silently change state and produce elusive bugs. You will also practice preventing infinite loops by designing clear loop exit conditions and ensuring loop variables are updated correctly. Another objective is applying control flow to small game scenarios: checking player status to display Health states, using switch to route menu choices, and iterating over enemies to update or remove them. Finally, you will build and run a short console exercise — the Guess the Number game — which combines a loop with conditional hints and shows how break can end a successful run. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm you can write, read, and reason about the control flow you produce in a C++ console context.

keyIdea.title: Practice focus
keyIdea.text: Safety checks and scenario-based practice prevent common bugs and build confident application of control flow in game code.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Practice & Safety
Objective focus

Safe comparisons and loop exits

Small mistakes like using assignment instead of equality or missing an increment can cause wrong behavior or infinite loops. Practice writing explicit checks and updating counters reliably.

Mnemonic
Check then change. Compare values before making assignments that alter state.
Scenario
Loop until player guesses correctly, but limit attempts to avoid infinite waiting.
Verified competency

You should be able to explain and identify off-by-one mistakes, write a loop with a safe exit, and choose the correct branching structure for a menu or state check.

screens.title: If statements — the simplest branch
screens.subtitle: Run code only when a condition is true

narration.text: An if statement evaluates a condition and executes a single block when that condition is true. This is the fundamental branching mechanism in C++. Think of it as a gate that opens for a single condition. A common game example is checking if player health is zero or below. If that check is true, you can print a Game Over message or trigger a respawn. The chapter shows this minimal example using playerHealth and a message. Always write conditions that are clear and testable. In practice, a condition can use comparison operators like equal, not equal, less than, and greater than. You will frequently combine these with logical AND and OR to express compound conditions. A common misconception is that an if can run multiple times like a loop — it cannot. If only one evaluation is required, use if. If you need repeated checks until a condition changes, use a loop. Concrete example: checking playerHealth <= 0 then printing a defeat notice. A short test you can try is setting playerHealth to different values and verifying which message runs. Takeaway: if handles single conditional execution; use it whenever a one-time decision is needed.

keyIdea.title: If summary
keyIdea.text: Use if for single-condition checks; it runs a block only when the condition evaluates to true.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › If statement
Definition

If — single conditional execution

Use when you need to run a block only if one condition is true. Not a loop; it does not repeat.

Common operators used in conditions:
  • Equality and inequality: ==, !=
  • Comparisons: <, >, <=, >=
  • Logical combination: &&, ||, !
Concrete example
int playerHealth = 75;
if (playerHealth <= 0) {
  std::cout << "Player has been defeated! Game Over." << std::endl;
}
Common mistake
Using = instead of == changes the value instead of comparing it. That can silently alter program state and produce hard-to-find bugs.
Pro tip
Test boundary values like zero and negative health to ensure your condition covers edge cases.
Key Takeaway

If executes code once when a condition is true. Use it for single decisions such as handling death or unlocking a door.

narration.text: If-else and else-if chains let your program choose one among several exclusive actions. The first condition that evaluates to true runs and the rest are skipped. This is ideal for ranking systems, health statuses, or tiered responses. For example, you can map score ranges to ranks like Gold, Silver, or keep practicing. The pattern reads top-to-bottom, so the order matters — place the highest-threshold checks first. One common improvement is to write conditions so they are mutually exclusive and avoid redundant checks; this makes reasoning and maintenance easier. A common misconception is thinking else-if conditions are evaluated independently. They are conditional only when previous checks fail, so later checks can assume earlier ones were false and therefore simplify logic. Concrete exercise: supply a playerScore and test ranges: if score >= 2000 then Gold, else if >= 1000 then Silver, else practice more. Another practical tip: use comments to clarify exclusive ranges to prevent accidental overlap. Takeaway: use ordered else-if chains to select exactly one matching action from multiple possibilities. If-else and else-if chains means else-if chains test conditions in order; the first true condition wins, so order and exclusivity matter.. In practical terms, provide alternatives and ordered checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ordered checks
keyIdea.text: Else-if chains test conditions in order; the first true condition wins, so order and exclusivity matter.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Else-if chains
Pattern

Choose one action among many

Place conditions from most specific to least specific and rely on the fact that later checks only run if earlier ones were false.

Example
int playerScore = 1200;
if (playerScore >= 2000) {
  std::cout << "You achieved a Gold rank!" << std::endl;
} else if (playerScore >= 1000) {
  std::cout << "You achieved a Silver rank!" << std::endl;
} else {
  std::cout << "Keep practicing for a higher rank!" << std::endl;
}
Misconception
Placing ranges out of order can cause higher tiers to never be reached. Always check the largest thresholds first if using greater-than comparisons.
Quick check
Rewrite an overlapping chain so each case is exclusive. For example, use else-if with descending thresholds or use range checks that avoid overlap.
Key Takeaway

Else-if chains make single-choice decisions among many conditions; order them deliberately.

screens.title: Switch statements
screens.subtitle: A clean alternative for many discrete cases

narration.text: Switch statements evaluate an expression and jump to the matching case label, which is useful when you have distinct integer or enumerated choices such as menu selections. The example in this chapter shows playerChoice values that map to Attack, Defend, or Use Item. A critical point when using switch is the break keyword. Without break, execution falls through to subsequent cases, often producing unintended behavior. You can use fall-through intentionally in special cases, but it is a common source of bugs when accidental. Another recommended practice is to provide a default case to handle unexpected values, for example printing Invalid choice. Switch statements are typically clearer than long else-if chains when matching many discrete values because they group cases visually and reduce repeated condition expressions. In game code, switch is helpful for handling menu input or action IDs coming from UI events. Concrete example: a switch that prints which action the player chose and uses break to stop after the matching block. Misconception to avoid: believing switch compares ranges; it matches specific discrete values. For ranged checks, use if-else chains instead.

keyIdea.title: Switch summary
keyIdea.text: Switch is best for matching distinct values; always use break to prevent accidental fall-through and include a default case.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Switch statement
When to use

Discrete-choice branching

Use switch when the value you check can take a limited set of known discrete values. It reads better than many else-if checks for this case.

Example
int playerChoice = 2; // 1 Attack, 2 Defend, 3 Use Item
switch (playerChoice) {
    case 1:
        std::cout << "Player attacks!" << std::endl;
        break;
    case 2:
        std::cout << "Player defends!" << std::endl;
        break;
    case 3:
        std::cout << "Player uses an item!" << std::endl;
        break;
    default:
        std::cout << "Invalid choice." << std::endl;
        break;
}
Watch out
Dropping break causes fall-through, which often leads to multiple case blocks running unintentionally. Only use fall-through when intentionally combining logic between cases.
Pro tip
Use enums or named constants for case labels to improve readability and avoid magic numbers in your switch statements.
Key Takeaway

Switch is concise for exact matches. Use break to stop execution and default to catch unexpected values.

screens.title: For loop fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Repeat a known number of times

narration.text: The for loop is the go-to structure when you know how many times you want to repeat a block. It combines initialization, a loop condition, and an increment step into a compact form. Typical game uses include spawning a set number of enemies or iterating across array indices. The chapter example shows spawning five enemies using for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++), where the loop runs five times and i starts at zero. Two common mistakes are off-by-one errors and forgetting to update the loop variable. Off-by-one errors occur when the upper bound is inclusive instead of exclusive, resulting in one extra iteration or missing the last element. Forgetting to increment i can create an infinite loop. When iterating collections, prefer using the collection's size in the condition. Always test boundary cases: zero iterations, one iteration, and the expected maximum. A practical debugging tip is to print the loop index to verify the exact number of iterations at runtime. Takeaway: use for when the iteration count is known and be deliberate about inclusive versus exclusive bounds. For loop fundamentals means use for loops for known counts; watch off-by-one errors and ensure loop variables change to avoid infinite loops.. In practical terms, repeat a known number of times. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: For summary
keyIdea.text: Use for loops for known counts; watch off-by-one errors and ensure loop variables change to avoid infinite loops.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › For loop
Structure

Initialization · Condition · Increment

Use when you know how many iterations you need. Count from zero when indexing arrays or tiles to avoid off-by-one errors.

Example — spawn enemies
// Simulate spawning 5 enemies
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    std::cout << "Spawning enemy #" << (i + 1) << std::endl;
}
Common error
Using i <= 5 when you intended 5 iterations starting at zero will run six times. Prefer i < count when counting from zero.
Debugging tip
Print the loop index and the condition to confirm how many iterations actually occur under different inputs.
Key Takeaway

For loops are for fixed counts. Pick bounds carefully and ensure the increment makes progress toward loop termination.

narration.text: A while loop repeats a block as long as its condition remains true, and is ideal when you don't know how many iterations are needed. Typical uses include waiting for input or running a main game loop until a boolean like isGameOver flips. The chapter example shows decrementing enemiesRemaining until it reaches zero. The crucial safety concern with while is infinite loops: if the condition never becomes false, the program will continue indefinitely, consuming C P U and possibly freezing. Always ensure the loop body updates state toward termination. That may be a decrementing counter, an input-driven flag, or a break statement triggered under special conditions. Another useful pattern is to place a maximum-iteration safeguard in complex loops as a defensive measure. Misconception: a while loop always runs at least once — that is false; it only runs if the condition is true initially. For guaranteed-at-least-once execution, use do-while. Practice: write a while loop for enemiesRemaining and test with different starting counts and with a missing decrement to observe the infinite-loop behavior intentionally. Takeaway: while is flexible but demands careful exit planning.

keyIdea.title: While summary
keyIdea.text: While repeats until its condition is false; ensure the loop body moves state toward termination to avoid infinite loops.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › While loop
When to use

Repeat until a condition changes

Use while when the number of iterations is unknown and depends on runtime events like player actions or incoming network messages.

Example
int enemiesRemaining = 3;
while (enemiesRemaining > 0) {
    std::cout << "Enemy defeated! " << enemiesRemaining << " remaining." << std::endl;
    enemiesRemaining--; // Update ensures termination
}
std::cout << "All enemies cleared!" << std::endl;
Safety note
If you forget to update the counter or change the condition, the loop becomes infinite. Always verify the transition that will make the condition false.
Defensive pattern
Consider adding a maximum-iteration counter inside complex while loops to bail out if something goes wrong.
Key Takeaway

While runs while a condition is true. Ensure the loop body makes progress toward termination to avoid infinite execution.

screens.title: Do-while loop
screens.subtitle: Run then check — execute at least once

narration.text: The do-while loop guarantees the loop body runs once before the condition is checked. This makes it useful for menus or input prompts where you need to display a prompt and then decide whether to repeat based on the response. The chapter example prompts the user to press Q to quit, ensuring the prompt appears at least once. Because the condition is evaluated after the body, be careful that the loop's logic still updates state properly to avoid accidental infinite repetition. Another misconception is treating do-while as identical to while; it is not. Use do-while when the first execution must happen unconditionally, then repeat only if the condition holds. A practical test is to run the loop when the initial input already satisfies the exit condition and verify it still runs once. When writing console input loops, validate and sanitize input within the loop to avoid unexpected behavior. Takeaway: use do-while when you want guaranteed initial execution followed by conditional repetition. Do-while loop means use do-while when the body must execute at least once before checking the loop condition.. In practical terms, run then check — execute at least once. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Do-while summary
keyIdea.text: Use do-while when the body must execute at least once before checking the loop condition.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Do-while loop
Behavior

Execute once, then repeat if true

Useful for an input prompt or a menu where you must show options at least once and then repeat based on a response.

Example
char playerInput;
do {
    std::cout << "Press 'Q' to quit: ";
    std::cin >> playerInput;
} while (playerInput != 'Q' && playerInput != 'q');
std::cout << "Exiting game loop." << std::endl;
Misconception
Do not assume do-while is interchangeable with while. Use it only when initial execution is required regardless of the condition.
Practical tip
For console input, validate input inside the loop before using it to avoid processing invalid values in the first iteration.
Key Takeaway

Do-while guarantees one execution before the condition is checked. Use it for prompts or menus that must appear first.

narration.text: Break and continue let you change the normal sequence of loop execution. Break immediately terminates the innermost loop or a switch statement and resumes execution after it. Continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and proceeds to the next one. Both are useful in game logic: use continue to skip disabled enemies when iterating a list, and break when you find the target and no longer need to check further. The chapter provides a concrete for-loop example showing how continue skips printing the value three, and break ends the loop when i equals seven, producing output 0 1 2 4 5 6. A common misconception is to overuse break and continue instead of structuring loop conditions clearly — excessive use can make loops harder to read. Use them judiciously for early exits and iteration skipping, and prefer clear loop conditions where possible. When using nested loops, remember break only exits the innermost loop unless additional control is implemented. Takeaway: break exits the loop early, continue skips to the next iteration; both help manage complex iteration logic efficiently. Break and continue means use break to stop loops early and continue to skip to the next iteration; apply them where they make the loop clearer and more efficient.. In practical terms, alter loop execution mid-way. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop control
keyIdea.text: Use break to stop loops early and continue to skip to the next iteration; apply them where they make the loop clearer and more efficient.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Break & Continue
What they do

Exit early or skip an iteration

Use break to stop searching once you find what you need. Use continue to avoid processing unwanted entries but keep iterating.

Example
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i == 3) {
        continue; // Skip printing 3
    }
    if (i == 7) {
        break; // Exit loop when i is 7
    }
    std::cout << i << " ";
}
// Output: 0 1 2 4 5 6
Nested loops note
Break only exits the innermost loop. To exit multiple layers, consider flags or structured control flow outside the loops.
When to avoid
Avoid using break and continue to patch unclear loop conditions. Prefer clearer loop predicates when possible for maintainability.
Key Takeaway

Break and continue let you control loop flow precisely. Use them for efficient searches and skipping undesired iterations.

screens.title: Combining loops and conditionals for game logic
screens.subtitle: Iterate entities and make decisions per entity

narration.text: Real game logic often composes loops that iterate sets of entities with conditionals inside each iteration. For example, you might loop through enemies and check whether each one is alive, disabled, or should be removed. Inside the loop you can continue to skip disabled enemies and break if a boss triggers a special event that halts the sweep. The important design considerations are clear ordering, minimal side effects, and predictable termination. Use descriptive variable names and keep each loop body focused: check status, update position, apply damage, and remove from a collection if needed. A common pitfall is modifying the collection you are iterating without handling index shifts, which can skip elements or cause out-of-range errors. Use careful index management or iterate backwards when removing elements, or collect removals and process them after the loop. The chapter recommends patterns like skipping disabled entities with continue and stopping early with break when appropriate. Concrete scenario: iterate enemies, skip if isDisabled, apply damage otherwise, and break if targetFound. Takeaway: structure your loop bodies to make decisions predictable and safe when applied to entity lists.

keyIdea.title: Practical pattern
keyIdea.text: When iterating entities, skip disabled ones and handle removals safely to avoid skipped or duplicated processing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Loop + Conditional Pattern
Pattern

Iterate entities and branch per item

Process each game entity with focused checks: skip if disabled, update if active, and remove when finished. Manage removals carefully to avoid index errors.

Scenario
For each enemy: if disabled, continue. Apply movement and damage. If enemy health <= 0, mark for removal or remove safely after the loop.
Pitfall
Removing items while iterating forward can skip the next item. Iterate backwards or collect indices to remove after the loop.
Best practice
Keep loop bodies short and side-effect-free where possible. Use helper functions to encapsulate complex per-entity logic.
Key Takeaway

Compose loops and conditionals to process game entities safely. Avoid in-loop modifications that change indexing unexpectedly.

screens.title: Guess the Number — hands-on console example
screens.subtitle: Combine loops, conditionals, and break in a small program

narration.text: The Guess the Number activity ties together loops and conditionals into a small playable program. The chapter gives starter code that hardcodes a secret number and then uses either a for loop with a maximum number of guesses or a while loop to continue until the player guesses correctly. In the provided example, a for loop runs up to five attempts. Inside the loop you read the player's guess, compare it to the secret, and give feedback: Too low, Too high, or Correct. When the guess is correct, set a flag and break to exit the loop early. After the loop, check the flag and reveal whether the player won or ran out of guesses. This example reinforces many ideas: choosing the right loop type for a limited attempt count, using if-else-if for multi-way feedback, and break to exit on success. A common extension challenge is replacing the hardcoded secret with a random generator later. When you implement this exercise, compile and run it, try edge inputs, and ensure that input handling does not leave the program waiting unexpectedly. Takeaway: building small programs like this grounds abstract control flow in clear runtime behavior and immediate feedback.

keyIdea.title: Practice program
keyIdea.text: The Guess the Number exercise demonstrates combining loops, conditionals, and break to implement interactive console logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Guess the Number
Starter code
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    const int SECRET_NUMBER = 7;
    int playerGuess;
    int guessCount = 0;
    const int MAX_GUESSES = 5;
    bool hasGuessedCorrectly = false;

    std::cout << "Welcome to Guess the Number!" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 10." << std::endl;

    for (guessCount = 0; guessCount < MAX_GUESSES; guessCount++) {
        std::cout << "Guess #" << (guessCount + 1) << "/" << MAX_GUESSES << ". Enter your guess: ";
        std::cin >> playerGuess;

        if (playerGuess == SECRET_NUMBER) {
            std::cout << "Congratulations! You guessed the secret number " << SECRET_NUMBER << "!" << std::endl;
            hasGuessedCorrectly = true;
            break;
        } else if (playerGuess < SECRET_NUMBER) {
            std::cout << "Too low! Try again." << std::endl;
        } else {
            std::cout << "Too high! Try again." << std::endl;
        }
    }

    if (!hasGuessedCorrectly) {
        std::cout << "Sorry, you ran out of guesses! The secret number was " << SECRET_NUMBER << "." << std::endl;
    }

    std::cout << "Thanks for playing!" << std::endl;

    return 0;
}
What to test
  • Correct guess on first try
  • Too low and too high hints
  • Exhausting the maximum guesses
Challenge
Replace the hardcoded secret with a random generator after you master srand and rand, and add input validation to avoid non-numeric input problems.
Key Takeaway

Small projects combine control flow patterns into meaningful behavior and reveal common mistakes to fix.

narration.text: Choosing the appropriate loop makes code clearer and less error-prone. Use for when you can determine the iteration count in advance, such as spawning five enemies or iterating an array by index. Use while when repetition depends on a condition that may change due to input or external events, like running a main loop until isGameOver becomes true. Use do-while when you must execute body logic at least once, such as prompting a player for input and then repeating if they didn't quit. Each has a distinct idiom: for expresses initialization, condition, and increment compactly; while emphasizes the condition up front; do-while emphasizes the body first. Misconceptions include overusing one loop form for all cases; this can hide intent and introduce bugs such as off-by-one errors with for or missing initial execution with while. A practical comparison: implement the same enemy update using each construct and observe behavior differences for zero initial enemies, one enemy, and many enemies. Takeaway: pick the loop form that matches your intent — clarity reduces bugs and improves maintainability. Choosing the right loop means match the loop type to your intent: known count → for, condition-driven → while, guaranteed-first-run → do-while.. In practical terms, for vs while vs do-while. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop choice
keyIdea.text: Match the loop type to your intent: known count → for, condition-driven → while, guaranteed-first-run → do-while.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Loop comparison
For
Best when count is known. Compact form expresses loop variables and progression.
While
Best when repetition depends on a condition that may change at runtime.
Do-while
Guarantees at least one execution before checking the condition, ideal for prompts.
Practical test
Try the same enemy update with each loop type and test zero, one, and many enemies to see how initial conditions affect execution.

narration.text: These are the core concepts you should remember from this chapter. Control flow is the order in which statements execute. Conditional statements let you run code only when a condition is true, using if, else-if, and else to choose actions. The switch statement is for matching discrete values and should include break statements to avoid fall-through and a default to handle unexpected values. Each of these concepts appears in short code examples in the chapter. Keep these definitions handy while you code and use them as a checklist when reading or writing conditional logic. Key Concepts — Part 1 means remember the difference between conditional checks and loops, and use the right structure for the job.. In practical terms, core terms and short definitions. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory aid
keyIdea.text: Remember the difference between conditional checks and loops, and use the right structure for the job.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Key Concepts
Control Flow
Order in which statements execute or are evaluated.
Conditional Statement
Runs code only when a condition is true (if / else-if / else).
Loop
Repeats a block: for, while, do-while.
Summary: Use conditionals to choose, loops to repeat, and loop controls to manage execution precisely.

narration.text: Finish with a few concise reminders. Break terminates the innermost loop or switch immediately and is useful for early exits. Continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next one, which is handy for filtering out disabled entities without nested conditions. Beware of infinite loops when loop conditions never become false, and prefer explicit progress toward loop termination. Finally, choose the loop type that communicates your intent: for for fixed counts, while for condition-driven repetition, and do-while when you must execute at least once. Practicing these patterns in short console programs like Guess the Number helps solidify their behavior and exposes common errors to fix. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Key Concepts
Break
Terminate the innermost loop or switch immediately.
Continue
Skip the rest of the current iteration and move to the next.
Infinite Loop
Occurs when a loop's condition never becomes false; ensure progress toward termination.
Final takeaway: write clear conditions, choose the right loop, and guard against common mistakes. Practice with small console programs to build confidence.
